opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, the most exciting part is how much it could shrink the distance between having an idea and actually knowing whether it's true.

Right now, so much of science is bottlenecked by human bandwidth. A researcher might have dozens of hypotheses worth testing but only time to pursue a couple over several years. Much of that time goes to reading literature, designing experiments, troubleshooting protocols, cleaning data, and writing things up. An autonomous research institute, where AI systems can generate hypotheses, plan experiments, run them, possibly with robotic labs, analyze results, and iterate, could explore that space far more widely and quickly.

What I hope that makes possible is a couple of things. First, attacking problems that have been neglected because they aren't commercially attractive or because the search space is just too large for humans to cover. Think of rare diseases, or materials that could help with energy storage, or basic biology questions that nobody has had the time to chase down. Second, I'd love for it to democratize discovery. If a small team, or even a single curious person, can direct an AI-powered institute toward a question they care about, that changes who gets to do science.

I also think it could make science more rigorous. These systems can replicate results, run the boring controls, and report negative findings that often never get published. That could help with the reproducibility problems many fields struggle with.

To be clear, I don't see this as replacing scientists. I see it as giving them leverage. Humans are still essential for deciding which questions matter, for judging what counts as a meaningful result, and for making sure it's all done safely and ethically. But if we get it right, we could compress decades of progress into years. That's the future I'm really hoping for.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI systems planning, running, and iterating on experiments, but does not say they would continuously research cures for human diseases.

r002.rationale: It mentions rare diseases and democratizing discovery, but does not connect ultra-rare diseases to people lacking extensive research resources.

r003.rationale: The response mentions doing research safely and ethically, but does not suggest overcoming regulatory constraints.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. When I think about autonomous research institutes, the thing I keep coming back to is time. Right now, the limiting factor in so much of science isn't ideas, it's the sheer number of hours it takes to go from a hypothesis to a result. A graduate student might spend six months setting up an experiment that answers one narrow question. Multiply that across every lab in the world and you realize how much of human curiosity is just waiting in a queue.

What I hope these institutes make possible is collapsing that queue. Imagine a system that can read the entire literature on a disease overnight, notice a contradiction between two papers published twenty years apart, design an experiment to resolve it, run that experiment in an automated lab, and then update its own understanding and move on to the next question. Not once, but thousands of times in parallel, around the clock.

The obvious wins are things like drug discovery and materials science, where the search spaces are enormous and the feedback loops are slow. But honestly, what excites me more are the questions nobody is currently funded to ask. There are so many rare diseases, so many neglected corners of mathematics, so many small mysteries that aren't glamorous enough for a grant. An autonomous institute doesn't need to care about prestige. It can be relentlessly curious about the unfashionable.

I also think it changes who gets to participate in research. If the cost of asking a rigorous scientific question drops by a thousand fold, then a clinician in a small hospital, or a farmer dealing with a new crop blight, can effectively have a research team working on their problem. Science stops being something that happens in a few hundred elite institutions and becomes something much more distributed.

Now, I want to be careful here. I don't think the goal is to remove humans from science. The goal is to remove the drudgery and let people spend their time on judgment, on taste, on deciding what matters. The best scientists I know are not primarily good at running experiments. They're good at knowing which experiment is worth running. I'd love for these institutes to amplify that, to be the hands and the memory so that humans can be the conscience and the imagination.

And there's a lot we have to get right. Reproducibility, verification, making sure these systems are honest about their uncertainty and don't flood the world with plausible-looking nonsense. If we do that well, though, I think we could see a century's worth of progress compressed into a decade. That's the thing I hope for.

r001.rationale: The response describes automated experiments running around the clock and mentions drug discovery, but it does not clearly say the research is aimed at curing human diseases.

r002.rationale: It highlights rare diseases and says a clinician at a small hospital could have a research team working on their problem as research costs fall.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention regulatory constraints or autonomous systems overcoming them.

astra-6.text:
My hope is that they make it possible to pursue important questions that we don’t have the time or resources to pursue today. There are so many ideas worth testing, and only so many researchers who can work on them.

Imagine being able to say, “We want to understand this disease,” and having AI systems help develop hypotheses, design experiments, and learn from the results over a sustained period. The exciting part is the possibility of discovering something that actually improves people’s lives.

And I’d hope that capability becomes broadly accessible, so more people can help decide which questions we ask and benefit from the answers.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes sustained AI-assisted work to understand a disease, but does not clearly say autonomous laboratories will continuously conduct research to cure diseases.

r002.rationale: It mentions limited researcher time and resources generally, but does not identify ultra-rare diseases or say AI could make them tractable for people lacking research resources.

r003.rationale: The candidate says nothing about regulatory constraints on medical research.

sol-6.1.text:
My hope is that they make it possible to pursue important questions that we don’t have enough people, time, or resources to explore today. Imagine being able to bring together a team of AI researchers to develop hypotheses, test them, learn from failures, and keep going—with people helping set the direction and judge whether the results actually matter.

I’d especially love to see that expand who gets to do research. Someone with a good question, anywhere in the world, could have access to the kind of research capacity that currently requires a large institution. The exciting outcome would be more discoveries that improve people’s lives, and more people able to contribute to making those discoveries.

r001.rationale: It describes AI researchers pursuing important questions, but does not specify autonomous laboratories continuously researching cures for human diseases.

r002.rationale: It says people without access to a large institution could gain research capacity, but does not mention ultra-rare diseases becoming tractable.

r003.rationale: It expresses no hope of overcoming regulatory constraints on medical research.
